prime.problem: "Claude Code is slower than Claude" is a confusion of model and harness. One request to an agent becomes a loop of model calls and tool runs, and each call pays its own start and writing time. Without seeing the loop you optimise tokens/s when the real cost is the call count.
prime.fits: Second multiplier card. The per-call formula from the overview now repeats N times with tool time between. Context growth, next, shows that each call in the loop also gets bigger.
prime.goal: Compute an agent loop's total time from its calls, and decide when a loop is worth it.

attend: What does the harness do between two model calls, and what does it send back?
In the 4-call FizzBuzz loop, how much of the 13.43 s is waiting for first tokens, how much is writing, and how much is tools?
Why does running a harness on a local model hurt most?
Why does the loop win on real multi-step work but lose on FizzBuzz?

must: The harness wraps the model in a loop → call, run a tool, send back the result, call again → each call pays its own TTFT and writing time → total ≈ N × TTFT + total output ÷ speed + tool time
Per call the model is the same speed → per task the number of calls multiplies the cost → for a one-shot question a single call wins (3.66 s vs 13.43 s, 3.7×)
Each tool result is checked against reality → the task ends up done, not just answered → for multi-step work (read, edit, test, retry) the loop beats you as the tool runner
elevated: Every call re-sends the growing history as its prompt → prefill on each call → cheap with prompt caching on a fast host, very expensive on a laptop's prefill speed

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the agent loop as a cycle with the four boxes (you, model call, tool runs, answer) and label what each arrow carries. Then compute the 4-call loop's time from its parts and one sentence on when a raw call is better.
checklist: model call → tool call request → tool runs → result + whole history re-sent → next call
4 × 1.39 s waiting + 480 ÷ 66 s writing + 0.6 s tools ≈ 13.43 s
raw call better for one-shot questions with nothing to check
speed an agent up by cutting calls before chasing tokens/s

retrieve.q: Explain the difference between a model and a harness, and why the same model can take 3.66 s or 13.43 s for FizzBuzz.
answer: the model predicts tokens; the harness decides how many times to call it and runs tools between
the loop makes 4 calls plus tools: 13.43 s

retrieve.q: Walk through call 2 of the loop: what is in its prompt, what does it output, what runs after it, and how long does each part take?
answer: prompt: system prompt + request + call 1's output + the write-file result
output: 100 tokens asking to run python fizzbuzz.py: 1.39 + 100 ÷ 66 ≈ 2.91 s
the tool runs: 0.5 s; running total 7.93 s

retrieve.q: Your agent takes 40 calls for a task you think needs 10. Which would you try first: a faster host, clearer instructions, or turning thinking off? Justify with the loop formula.
answer: clearer instructions: cutting N cuts every term (TTFT, writing, prefill, tools)
a faster host only cuts the writing term
thinking off helps only if calls think a lot, and risks wrong steps

compare.q: Thinking and extra calls both multiply time. Which one multiplies tokens inside a call and which multiplies calls, and which one also brings a check against reality?
answer: thinking adds hidden tokens within one call
the harness adds whole calls, each with its own TTFT
only the harness loop runs tools, so only it can check work against reality

compare.q: The scheduler's token loop runs inside one model call (prefill, then decode per token); the harness loop runs across calls. What does each loop repeat, and which one's cost you can cut by editing a prompt?
answer: token loop: one decode step per output token, inside the server
harness loop: one full call (prefill + decode) per step, outside the server
prompt wording can cut both: fewer calls and fewer output tokens

predict.q: Run the same 4-call loop on your M3 with qwen3.5:4b (15.4 t/s) and a 5,000-token system prompt that is not cached. Predict whether the total is dominated by writing, tools or prefill. Commit before revealing.
predict.answer: Prefill. Each call reads at least 5,000 tokens at about 207 t/s ≈ 24 s, so 4 calls ≈ 97 s of reading, against 480 ÷ 15.4 ≈ 31 s of writing and 0.6 s of tools. That's why a harness on a local model hurts most, and why caching the prefix matters.

apply.task: Watch a real agent session (Claude Code, Cursor or your own script) for one small task. Count the model calls, note which tool ran between each, and estimate each call's output tokens. Compute the loop total with the formula using your model's TTFT and speed, and compare with the wall-clock time.
apply.done: You have a per-call table, a computed total within about 30% of the real time, and one change that would cut the call count.
apply.hint: Claude Code's transcript shows each tool use; each one sits between two model calls.
